headline: Australian rental market facing decades-worst conditions with rents surging $100–$300 per week in sub-million-dollar markets, SMSF borrowing changes could add further pressure
reasoning: Sam Gordon highlights that rents in many sub-million-dollar capital city markets have risen by $100 to $300 per week over the past 12 months, which he describes as some of the most severe rental conditions seen in decades. This surge is generating FOMO among renters, pushing them toward buying, which in turn adds to demand pressure at the lower end of the purchase market. The episode headline also references potential SMSF borrowing changes as an additional factor that could reduce rental supply and further tighten an already stretched rental market, though this point was not fully elaborated in the available transcript.
quote: We're seeing rents surging. So I think that's the first thing to really weigh in the equation is in a lot of locations right now, particularly sub million dollar markets, we're seeing rents rise anywhere between 100 to $300 a week in some capital cities, literally happening right now from where rents were at 12 months ago to right now. So it's almost like a fair amount of FOMO coming into the marketplace, fear of missing out of people going, well, if I can't get a rental now at 100 $100 a week increase, where is it going to be in 12 months? And so there's creating this huge pressure of those same renters and people who are looking to move out of living with potentially at home with mum and dad to go out there and rent their first property.
episode_title: Down at the top, hot at the bottom - housing's great divide | the advisory

headline: Bottom end of Australian property market remains fiercely competitive despite headline price falls, driven by government deposit scheme and surging rents
reasoning: Sam Gordon argues that while headlines suggest the Australian property market is falling broadly, the reality on the ground at the sub-million-dollar end is very different. The 5% deposit guarantee scheme introduced on 1 October 2025 created immediate and sustained demand from first home buyers. Rents in many locations have surged $100–$300 per week over the past 12 months, generating FOMO and pushing more renters toward purchasing. Investors, squeezed out of higher price points by the removal of negative gearing, are now competing at the same price points as first home buyers, intensifying competition. Vacancy rates at this tier are exceptionally tight and Gordon expects conditions to intensify further over the next 6–12 months.
quote: The very real reality out there right now is that bottom end of the market where first home buyers are specifically with the 5% deposit caps are in place. It's very, very fierce that those price points are still strong, the market is still strong, there's not a lot of stock. And you know, investors are being pushed down pricing wise with negative gearing being pulled out of the equation, which a lot of them were using for borrowing. And so now there's a lot of competition at the same price point. And it's at the same price point and at the same level as well, where vacancy rates are exceptionally tight, where most are most average Australians are sort of renting in that proximity and parameters as well. So not only are rents increasing in one of the most fierce rental conditions we've seen in decades, but at the same time, everyone's sort of being funnelled down to the same price point as well.
episode_title: Down at the top, hot at the bottom - housing's great divide | the advisory

headline: Top and middle end of Australian property market falling as sentiment deteriorates and buyers trade down rather than up
reasoning: Sam Gordon explains that the top end of the market performs well only when sentiment is high and conditions are strong; when sentiment turns negative, buyers refuse to trade up and instead look to trade down. This cascading effect is pushing demand progressively lower through the price spectrum. Owners at the top end who don't need to sell are withdrawing listings, while forced sellers are accepting serious discounts. Because the top end rose so sharply in the prior cycle, its correction distorts the median and makes the overall market look worse than it is at the lower end.
quote: The big thing with the top end of the market is when times are good, you know, these sorts of markets, these sorts of locations, they sort of do quite well. Right. When times are good and sentiment is very high when they're not like it's when times are bad, when sentiment is very low. People don't look to trade up. They look to trade down. And so, you know, seeing a lot of the top end people can't afford it. They're not willing to spend that top end dollar, especially when the economy's looking shakier and the housing market is looking shaky. They're not looking to go and buy that real top end price point. And we're even seeing in the middle as well. We're seeing those people looking to trade down center. When sentiment shifts, people don't trade up. I think that's a big thing. They continually trading down. So we're seeing it push more and more down. I think the headlines are making it look really bad, and the headlines are looking like the market is falling right across the country because we're seeing that top end come down.
episode_title: Down at the top, hot at the bottom - housing's great divide | the advisory
